topicsovertime

An R implementation of the Topics over Time (TOT) model of Wang and McCallum (2006).

TOT is an LDA-style topic model in which every topic has, besides its distribution over words, a Beta distribution over continuous time. Topics are found jointly from word co-occurrence and from when documents were written:

  • Time is neither discretized nor modeled with Markov dynamics, so there is no time-slice size to choose.
  • The meaning (word distribution) of a topic stays constant. What changes over time is how often each topic occurs.
  • A fitted model can predict when an undated document was written.

Inference uses collapsed Gibbs sampling written in C++ (via Rcpp).

Documentation: https://sorrychoe.github.io/topicsovertime/

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("sorrychoe/topicsovertime")

Usage

tot() takes a document-term matrix of counts (base matrix, a Matrix sparse matrix, a quanteda dfm, or a tm DocumentTermMatrix) and one timestamp per document (numeric, Date or POSIXct).

library(topicsovertime)
library(quanteda)

toks <- tokens(data_corpus_inaugural, remove_punct = TRUE, remove_numbers = TRUE)
toks <- tokens_remove(tokens_tolower(toks), stopwords("en"))
x <- dfm_trim(dfm(toks), min_termfreq = 5)
year <- docvars(data_corpus_inaugural, "Year")

set.seed(2026)
fit <- tot(x, year, k = 8, n_iter = 300)

fit                      # summary of the model
terms(fit, 10)           # top words per topic
fit$psi                  # Beta parameters of each topic (normalized time)
plot(fit)                # topic proportions over time, P(topic | time)
plot(fit, type = "density")  # Beta density of each topic over time

topic_time(fit, c(1800, 1900, 2000))      # P(topic | time) at given times
predict(fit, x, type = "topics")          # topic proportions of documents
predict(fit, x, type = "time")            # predicted year of each document

To try the model without any text data, simulate_tot() generates a synthetic corpus from known topics and time distributions.

Main functions

Function Description
tot() Fit the model by collapsed Gibbs sampling
terms() Most probable words per topic
topic_time() Topic proportions at given times, P(z \| t) ∝ p(t \| ψ_z) P(z)
predict(type = "topics") Topic proportions of new documents (fold-in)
predict(type = "time") Predicted timestamps of new documents
plot() Topic trends or topic time densities
simulate_tot() Simulate a corpus from the TOT generative process

Choosing time_weight

Each word token carries its document’s timestamp, so a long document’s time counts many times in the likelihood. time_weight rescales the time likelihood against the words. The paper notes that this setting is sensitive and has to be tuned.

time_weight Effect
1 (default) The Gibbs sampler exactly as in the paper. With long documents, time can dominate: topics become narrow time periods with mixed words.
"inverse_length" 1 / N_d, the alternative suggested in the paper: each document’s timestamp counts once. Topics are driven mostly by words.
a value in between A compromise. On ~8,000 Korean news articles (about 200 tokens each), 0.3 gave coherent topics while still improving date prediction.

Inspect terms() and plot() under a few values, and, if timestamps matter for your question, check predict(type = "time") on held-out documents.

Implementation notes

The sampler follows the paper. Three details differ from a literal reading of it:

  • Beta density orientation. The paper’s conditional is printed as (1 - t)^(ψ1 - 1) t^(ψ2 - 1), which does not match the method-of-moments estimates it is paired with. This package uses the standard t^(ψ1 - 1) (1 - t)^(ψ2 - 1).
  • Time normalization. Timestamps are mapped onto [1e-4, 1 - 1e-4] rather than exactly [0, 1], so log densities stay finite for the earliest and latest documents.
  • Bounded Beta densities. After each method-of-moments update, both Beta shapes are kept at or above 1 (same mean, higher concentration). Without this, a topic could collapse onto the first and last documents with a U-shaped Beta(≈0, ≈0) density and stay locked there. The cost is that U-shaped topics (common early and late, rare in between) cannot be represented.

The hyper-parameters alpha (default 50 / k) and beta (default 0.1) are fixed, as in the paper. The number of topics k must be chosen by the user.

Citation

If you use this package, please cite the original paper:

Wang, X. and McCallum, A. (2006). Topics over time: a non-Markov continuous-time model of topical trends. Proceedings of the 12th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 424–433. https://doi.org/10.1145/1150402.1150450
